topic_tag: time for a four-machine bottling line to finish a run of jugs, paced by the filler's rate, with periodic drum changes
subskill: throughput of machines in sequence
prompt: A bottling line fills 3.7-liter water jugs. Every jug passes through four machines in this order: a rinser (24 seconds per jug), a filler, a capper (11 seconds per jug), and a labeler (38 seconds per jug). The filler pumps water at a constant 4.3 liters per minute and fills each jug completely. Each machine works on one jug at a time, and a jug moves on to the next machine as soon as it is finished and the next machine is empty. The filler starts the run with a full supply drum; after every 60 jugs it fills, it stops for 85 seconds while the drum is replaced, and then continues. At the start, the line is empty and 215 jugs are waiting at the rinser. To the nearest tenth of a minute, how many minutes after the first jug enters the rinser does the 215th jug leave the labeler?
explanation: The filler takes 3.7/4.3 minute = 51.63 seconds per jug, longer than any other machine, so it sets the pace. The first jug leaves the labeler after 24 + 51.63 + 11 + 38 = 124.63 seconds. Each later jug leaves 51.63 seconds after the one before it, except that the filler stops for 85 seconds after its 60th, 120th, and 180th jugs (3 drum changes; none is needed after the 215th). Total: 124.63 + 214(51.63) + 3(85) = 124.63 + 11,048.37 + 255 = 11,428.0 seconds = 190.47 minutes, or 190.5 to the nearest tenth. The option 191.3 adds 215 filler cycles to the first jug's trip, counting the first jug twice. The option 191.9 rounds 215/60 = 3.58 up to 4 drum changes. The option 255.3 uses 4.3/3.7 minute per jug (the pump rate inverted), 69.77 seconds per jug.
quantity_asked: minutes from the first jug entering the rinser to the 215th jug leaving the labeler: the first jug's pass through all four machines, 214 more filler cycles, and 3 drum changes.

distractor_kind.191.3: error path: first jug's pass (124.63 s) plus 215 filler cycles plus 3 drum changes = 191.33 min (first jug counted twice). (a) no extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: one extra cycle, inside (0.86 min above the key). (c) inside every cheap estimate. (d) real fencepost error.
distractor_kind.191.9: error path: 215/60 = 3.58 drum changes rounded up to 4 = 191.88 min. (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) inside. (d) real counting error (a drum change after the last jug is not needed).
distractor_kind.255.3: error path: 4.3/3.7 min = 69.77 s per jug (liters per minute used as minutes per liter) through the same method = 255.33 min. (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) below the cheapest upper bound, 215 jugs at the full four-machine time each (446.6 min). (d) real inverted rate.

bounds: time > 215 x 51.63 s = 185.0 min: every jug must pass the filler
time < 215 x 124.63 s = 446.6 min plus drum changes: jugs handled one at a time through the whole line
mechanism: machines in sequence paced by the slowest machine
fill time from pump rate and jug volume
first item passes every machine
periodic stops after every 60 items
arith_class_check: No. All four are tenths of a minute with non-zero tenths; none is a multiple of a stem number.
one_sided_check: Key smallest. Distractors from three error kinds (fencepost, rounding the stop count up, inverted rate). Natural errors under the key: timing all 215 jugs at the filler pace without the first jug's trip through the other machines (189.3) and leaving out the drum changes (186.2); neither is an option.
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 191.3 and 191.9, both one-decimal minutes with non-zero tenths; neither is rounder.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bound: every jug passes the filler, so time > 215(51.63 s) = 185.0 min; all options exceed it. Upper: one jug at a time through the whole line, 446.6 min; all options are below it, so all three distractors lie on the key's side of it. The nearest distractor, 191.3, is 0.9 min above the key, finer than any estimate short of the full count.
trap_check: Clauses: "in this order ... one jug at a time" - ignoring the first jug's trip pushes DOWN (189.3, not an option), counting it twice pushes UP (191.3); "after every 60 jugs it fills" - leaving the stops out pushes DOWN (186.2, not an option), rounding 3.58 up pushes UP (191.9); "starts with a full supply drum" - adding a change before the first jug pushes UP (191.9, the same value); "4.3 liters per minute" - inverting pushes UP (255.3). At most one distractor per clause.

191.3.step: jug count after the first jug
191.3.error_type: other: fencepost, first jug counted twice

191.9.error_type: other: rounds the change count up

255.3.step: fill time per jug from the pump rate

counter_error.step: line fill (first jug's pass through the other machines)

stated_rules.rule: drum change of 85 s after every 60 jugs
filler starts with a full drum (no change before the first jug)
line starts empty (first jug passes all four machines)
one jug per machine, moves when the next machine is empty

self_audit.note: Smallest key; overs from fencepost, rounded-up stop count, inverted pump rate; natural unders (no line-fill time, stops left out) not options; stated rules split.

topic_tag: hours to finish a knitted blanket: squares still to knit plus sewing every shared edge
subskill: work rates with a count of shared edges
prompt: Ines is making a blanket from 48 identical knitted squares, each 9 inches on a side, arranged in 6 rows of 8 squares. She has already knitted 11 of the squares, but 3 of those came out too small and must be knitted again. She knits at a steady rate of one square every 32 minutes. When all 48 squares are ready, she will sew together every pair of squares that share an edge, along the whole 9-inch shared edge, and she sews at a steady 5 inches per minute. To the nearest hundredth of an hour, how many hours of knitting and sewing does Ines have left?
explanation: She must knit 48 - 11 + 3 = 40 more squares, taking 40(32) = 1,280 minutes. In 6 rows of 8, each row has 7 shared edges between neighbors (6 x 7 = 42), and each of the 8 columns has 5 shared edges (8 x 5 = 40), so there are 82 shared edges. Each takes 9/5 = 1.8 minutes to sew, so sewing takes 82(1.8) = 147.6 minutes. The total is 1,280 + 147.6 = 1,427.6 minutes = 23.79 hours. The option 20.59 subtracts the 3 squares to be redone instead of adding them (34 squares). The option 22.09 computes the time per edge as 5/9 minute instead of 9/5. The option 22.77 sews one edge per square (48 edges).
quantity_asked: hours left: 40 squares at 32 minutes each plus 82 shared 9-inch edges sewn at 5 inches per minute.

distractor_kind.20.59: error path: 48 - 11 - 3 = 34 squares left (the 3 redone squares subtracted). (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) inside: knitting alone for 40 squares is 21.33 h, but nothing in the stem gives a one-step bound that excludes 34 squares' worth. (d) real sign slip.
distractor_kind.22.09: error path: minutes per edge = 5/9 instead of 9/5 (82 edges take 45.6 minutes). (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) inside. (d) real inverted-rate error.
distractor_kind.22.77: error path: one shared edge per square, 48 edges. (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) inside. (d) real counting error (edges per square instead of shared edges in the grid).

bounds: hours > 0; knitting alone for the 40 squares is 21.33 hours
hours < 51(32)/60 + 110(1.8)/60 = 30.5 (every square knitted, every grid line sewn)
mechanism: knitting squares at a steady rate
counting shared edges in a rectangular grid
sewing rate in inches per minute
squares to redo added to the remaining work
arith_class_check: No. All four are two-decimal hours with non-zero hundredths; none is a stem number or a simple multiple of another.
one_sided_check: Key largest; distractors from three clauses and three kinds (sign slip on the redone squares, inverted sewing rate, one seam per square). Errors that push UP are as natural: forgetting the 11 finished squares gives 29.66, counting 2 seams per square (96) gives 24.21, and counting every grid line including the border (110) gives 24.63; so a student cannot tell from the stem that slips lower the answer.
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 22.09 and 22.77, both two-decimal hours with non-zero hundredths; neither is rounder.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bound: knitting alone, 40 x 32 minutes = 21.33 hours, is a lower bound; 22.09 and 22.77 lie above it on the key's side, and only 20.59 (which miscounts the squares) lies below it. The nearest distractor, 22.77, is 1.02 hours (4.3%) below the key; sewing time is the only part that separates them and no one-step estimate fixes it.
trap_check: Clauses: "already knitted 11" - ignoring it pushes UP (29.66, not an option); "3 of those ... knitted again" - subtracting them pushes DOWN (20.59), ignoring them pushes DOWN (22.19, not an option); "every pair of squares that share an edge" - one per square pushes DOWN (22.77), two per square or all grid lines pushes UP (24.21 / 24.63, not options); "5 inches per minute" with 9-inch edges - 5/9 minute per edge pushes DOWN (22.09). One distractor per clause; none from ignoring a clause.

stated_rules.rule: 11 squares already knitted
3 of those must be knitted again
sew every pair of squares that share an edge, full 9-inch edge
one square every 32 minutes; 5 inches per minute

self_audit.note: Largest key; under errors from three clauses (sign slip, inverted rate, edge count); natural UP errors: finished squares ignored, 96 or 110 seams counted.

topic_tag: hotel balance charged in euros using a cross rate built from two dollar quotes, after a euro deposit
subskill: cross exchange rate from two quotes
prompt: A currency website lists these exchange rates: 1 U.S. dollar = 0.9216 euro, and 1 U.S. dollar = 0.7848 British pound. Sofia, who lives in Spain, stayed 3 nights at a London hotel that charges 168 British pounds per night. When she booked the room, she paid a deposit of 140 euros, which the hotel credited toward her bill. At checkout, the hotel charged the rest of the bill, in pounds, to Sofia's card, and her bank converted that charge to euros. The hotel and the bank both converted between pounds and euros at the rate implied by the website's two rates, with no fees. To the nearest cent, how many euros did the bank charge Sofia at checkout?
explanation: One pound is worth 1/0.7848 dollar, and each dollar is worth 0.9216 euro, so 1 pound = 0.9216/0.7848 = about 1.1743 euros. The bill is 3(168) = 504 pounds, which is worth 504(0.9216/0.7848) = about 591.85 euros. The deposit of 140 euros was credited toward it, so the bank charged 591.85 - 140 = 451.85 euros. (Equivalently, the deposit is worth 140(0.7848/0.9216) = 119.22 pounds, the hotel charged 384.78 pounds, and 384.78 pounds is 451.85 euros.) The option 427.45 subtracts the deposit as if it were 140 pounds. The option 398.79 converts the 140-euro deposit to pounds by multiplying by 1.1743 instead of dividing. The option 556.83 converts the bill to dollars correctly but then divides by 0.9216 instead of multiplying to get euros.
quantity_asked: euros charged at checkout: the 504-pound bill in euros at 0.9216/0.7848 euro per pound, minus the 140-euro deposit.

distractor_kind.427.45: error path: the 140-euro deposit subtracted from the bill as 140 pounds, then the rest converted. (a) not a parameter extreme. (b) not an intermediate (the bill in euros is 591.85, the deposit in pounds 119.22). (c) inside every one-step estimate: euros owed must exceed 504 - 140 = 364 and be below 591.85. (d) real wrong-currency (wrong base) error.
distractor_kind.398.79: error path: the deposit converted to pounds with the rate the wrong way (140 x 1.1743 = 164.40 pounds), then the rest converted. (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) above the 364 floor and below 591.85; inside. (d) real inverted-rate error on the deposit step.
distractor_kind.556.83: error path: 504 pounds = 642.20 dollars correctly, then dollars to euros by dividing by 0.9216 instead of multiplying; minus 140. (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) inside 364 to 591.85. (d) real inverted-rate error on the second conversion.

427.45.error_kind: deposit subtracted in the wrong currency

398.79.error_kind: deposit converted with the rate inverted

556.83.error_kind: dollars to euros by division (rate inverted)

bounds: euros charged > 504 - 140 = 364, since a pound is worth more than a euro (0.7848 < 0.9216 pounds vs euros per dollar)
euros charged < 504 pounds in euros = 591.85, since the deposit is positive
mechanism: cross exchange rate from two dollar quotes
pounds to euros via dollars
deposit credited in another currency
hotel bill nights times nightly rate
arith_class_check: No. All four are two-decimal amounts with non-zero last digits (398.79, 427.45, 451.85, 556.83); none is a stem number times another, none is an integer.
one_sided_check: key interior
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 427.45 and 451.85, both two-decimal euro amounts with non-zero hundredths; neither is rounder.
cheap_bound_check: key interior
trap_check: Clauses: "deposit of 140 euros" - taking it as pounds pushes DOWN (427.45), ignoring it pushes UP (591.85, not an option); "1 dollar = 0.9216 euro" - dividing instead of multiplying pushes UP (556.83); "1 dollar = 0.7848 pound" - multiplying instead of dividing pushes DOWN (224.53, not an option); converting the deposit with the cross rate inverted pushes DOWN (398.79). At most one distractor from ignoring a clause: none comes from ignoring a clause.

stated_rules.rule: the 140-euro deposit is credited toward the bill
3 nights at 168 pounds per night
conversions at the rate implied by the two dollar quotes, no fees

self_audit.note: Interior key; two under errors (deposit currency, deposit inverted) and one over (euro quote inverted); no option violates the 364-591.85 bracket.

topic_tag: cost per 1,000 miles of a new set of tires with per-tire, per-car and rebate items
subskill: unit cost from mixed per-item and per-order charges
prompt: Dana buys a set of 4 tires at $138.75 per tire. Installation costs $22.00 per tire, except that the fourth tire is installed free. A wheel alignment costs $94.95 for the car. After the purchase, Dana receives a $70.00 mail-in rebate on the set. She drives 12,500 miles per year and will replace the tires after 4 years or 55,000 miles, whichever comes first. Counting the tires, installation, alignment, and rebate, what will Dana's tires cost per 1,000 miles driven on them, to the nearest cent?
explanation: The tires cost 4(138.75) = $555.00, installation is 3(22.00) = $66.00, and the alignment is $94.95, a total of $715.95; the rebate brings it to $645.95. In 4 years she drives 4(12,500) = 50,000 miles, which comes before 55,000 miles, so the tires are used for 50,000 miles. The cost per 1,000 miles is 645.95/50 = $12.92. The option 13.36 pays installation on all 4 tires. The option 15.72 adds the $70.00 rebate instead of subtracting it. The option 18.62 charges the alignment once per tire.
quantity_asked: dollars per 1,000 miles: (555 + 66 + 94.95 - 70) over 50 thousand miles.

distractor_kind.13.36: error path: installation paid on all 4 tires (the free fourth ignored). (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) 0.44 above the key, finer than any one-step estimate; strictly inside. (d) real omission of the free-installation condition.
distractor_kind.15.72: error path: the $70 rebate added to the cost. (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) inside. (d) real sign slip.
distractor_kind.18.62: error path: the $94.95 alignment charged for each of the 4 tires. (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) inside the 11-to-20 range of one-step estimates. (d) real error: a per-car charge treated as per-tire.

bounds: cost per 1,000 miles > (555 - 70)/55 = 8.82 (tires and rebate only, longest possible life)
mechanism: cost per 1,000 miles of tires
per-tire versus per-car charges
mail-in rebate
replacement after years or miles whichever first

Errors that push DOWN are as natural: using the 55,000-mile limit instead of the 50,000 miles actually driven gives 11.74, leaving out the alignment gives 11.02, and taking the $70 rebate off each tire gives 8.72; so the stem does not tell a student that slips raise the answer.

topic_tag: hours to haul topsoil when a weight limit, not the truck bed, sets the load size, with loader rate, loaded and empty speeds and no final return
subskill: rates with a binding capacity limit
prompt: A landscaper must haul 37 cubic yards of wet topsoil from a supply yard to a job site 11 miles away, using one truck. Wet topsoil weighs 2,300 pounds per cubic yard. The truck's bed holds up to 7 cubic yards, but the truck may carry at most 14,000 pounds of topsoil on any one load. At the yard, a loader puts topsoil into the truck at a rate of 0.55 cubic yard per minute, and at the job site each load takes 9 minutes to dump. The truck averages 40 miles per hour when loaded and 50 miles per hour when empty. The job starts when the loader begins filling the first load and ends when the last load has been dumped; the truck does not return to the yard after the last load. Every load except possibly the last carries as much topsoil as allowed. To the nearest hundredth of an hour, how long does the job take?
explanation: The weight limit allows 14,000/2,300 = 6.087 cubic yards per load, less than the 7-cubic-yard bed, so 37/6.087 = 6.08 loads means 7 loads are needed. Loading all 37 cubic yards takes 37/0.55 = 67.27 minutes in all (the last load is partial). Each of the 7 loads is driven 11 miles at 40 mph (16.5 minutes) and dumped (9 minutes): 7(25.5) = 178.5 minutes. The truck returns empty 6 times, 11 miles at 50 mph (13.2 minutes) each: 79.2 minutes. Total 67.27 + 178.5 + 79.2 = 324.97 minutes = 5.416, or 5.42, hours. The option 4.63 finds the loading time as 37(0.55) minutes (the loader rate inverted). The option 4.82 uses 6.08 loads instead of rounding up to 7. The option 5.35 uses the average of the two speeds, 45 mph, for every drive.
quantity_asked: total hours from the start of loading to the end of the last dump: loading time for 37 cubic yards, 7 loaded drives and dumps, 6 empty returns.

distractor_kind.4.63: error path: loading time 37 x 0.55 = 20.35 minutes (cubic yards per minute used as minutes per cubic yard). (a) no parameter extreme. (b) not an intermediate (load size 6.087, loads 6.08 / 7, loading 67.27 min, drive 16.5, return 13.2). (c) inside: above the 7 drives + dumps + 6 returns alone (4.30 h), below the key. (d) real inverted rate.
distractor_kind.4.82: error path: 6.08 loads (37/6.087) used without rounding up, so 6.08 loaded drives and dumps and 5.08 returns. (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) inside the interval; no one-step estimate separates it without the load count. (d) real error: fractional trip count.
distractor_kind.5.35: error path: every drive at the average speed 45 mph (14.67 minutes each way). (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) 0.07 h below the key, inside every cheap estimate. (d) real error: averaging the two speeds instead of using each for its leg.

5.35.error_kind: average of the two speeds for every leg

bounds: job > 4.30 h: 7 loaded drives and dumps plus 6 returns, before any loading time (needs the load count 7)
job < 5.64 h: the key with a 7th return trip added (the truck does not return)
mechanism: weight limit binds before truck bed volume
number of loads rounded up
loader rate cubic yards per minute
loaded and empty speeds
no return after the last load
arith_class_check: No. All four are hundredths with non-zero last digits; none is a multiple of a stem number or a clean fraction of an hour.
one_sided_check: Key largest. Distractors from three error kinds (inverted loader rate, fractional loads, averaged speed). Natural errors over the key: filling the partial last load as a full 6.087-cubic-yard load (5.59) and adding a return after the last load (5.64); neither is an option.
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 4.82 and 5.35, both two-decimal hours with non-zero last digits; neither is rounder.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bounds: with 7 loads, job > 7(16.5 + 9) + 6(13.2) minutes = 4.30 h, which every option exceeds; adding a 7th return gives 5.64 h, which every option is below, so all three distractors lie on the key's side of both. The nearest distractor, 5.35, is 0.07 h (4 minutes) below the key, inside any estimate short of the full sum.
trap_check: Clauses: "at most 14,000 pounds" - ignoring it (bed-limited, 6 loads) pushes DOWN (4.77, not an option); "0.55 cubic yard per minute" - inverting it pushes DOWN (4.63); "40 ... loaded and 50 ... empty" - averaging pushes DOWN (5.35); "does not return after the last load" - ignoring it pushes UP (5.64, not an option); "except possibly the last" - filling a full last load pushes UP (5.59, not an option); rounding loads up - skipping it pushes DOWN (4.82). One distractor per clause.

4.63.step: loading time from the loader rate

5.35.step: drive times for loaded and empty legs

counter_error.error_type: other: returns after the last load

stated_rules.rule: at most 14,000 pounds of topsoil per load
9 minutes to dump each load
no return to the yard after the last load
last load may be partial (loader time counts only soil actually loaded)
bed holds up to 7 cubic yards

topic_tag: end-to-end light-rail trip time with a slower graded section and station stops
subskill: multi-segment travel time with stops
prompt: A light-rail line runs 23.6 kilometers from one end station to the other and has 15 stations in all, including the two end stations. While moving, the train averages 46 kilometers per hour, except on a 4.8-kilometer section that climbs a steep grade, where its average speed while moving is 20% less than that. On each trip, the train stops for 35 seconds at every station other than the two end stations. To the nearest tenth of a minute, how many minutes does a trip take, from the moment the train leaves one end station until it arrives at the other?
explanation: On the grade the train averages 0.80(46) = 36.8 km/h, so that section takes 4.8/36.8 hour = 7.826 minutes. The other 23.6 - 4.8 = 18.8 km take 18.8/46 hour = 24.522 minutes. The train stops at the 15 - 2 = 13 stations between the end stations, for 13(35) = 455 seconds = 7.583 minutes. The trip takes 7.826 + 24.522 + 7.583 = 39.93, or 39.9 minutes. The option 39.6 finds the grade speed as 46/1.20 (20% less taken on the wrong base). The option 41.1 counts a 35-second stop at all 15 stations. The option 36.9 writes the 455 seconds of stops as 4.55 minutes.
quantity_asked: trip minutes: 18.8 km at 46 km/h plus 4.8 km at 36.8 km/h, plus 13 stops of 35 seconds.

distractor_kind.39.6: error path: grade speed 46/1.20 = 38.33 km/h (20% less on the wrong base). (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate. (c) inside: no one-step estimate resolves 0.3 minute. (d) real wrong-base percent error.
distractor_kind.41.1: error path: a 35-second stop counted at all 15 stations (525 seconds = 8.75 minutes of stops). (a) no extreme. (b) not the stop total (7.58) or the moving time (32.35). (c) inside the 30.8-to-47.2 minute bracket. (d) real counting error.
distractor_kind.36.9: error path: 455 seconds of stops written as 4.55 minutes. (a) no extreme. (b) not an intermediate value of the correct process (moving time 32.35). (c) inside. (d) real seconds-as-decimal-minutes error (the one min:sec slip in this run).

39.6.error_kind: percent less on the wrong base

41.1.error_kind: stops counted at end stations too

bounds: trip > moving time at 46 km/h over 23.6 km = 30.78 minutes
trip < 23.6 km at 36.8 km/h plus 15 stops = 47.2 minutes
mechanism: light-rail end-to-end trip time
station dwell time at intermediate stations
slower section percent less speed
kilometers per hour to minutes
arith_class_check: No. All four are tenths with non-zero last digits; none is a multiple of 35 seconds or of a stem number.
one_sided_check: key interior
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 39.6 and 39.9, both tenths with non-zero last digits; neither is rounder.
cheap_bound_check: key interior
trap_check: Clauses: "20% less" on the grade - using 46/1.2 pushes DOWN (39.6), ignoring it pushes DOWN (38.4, not an option), reading it as 20% more pushes DOWN (37.3, not an option); "stations other than the two end stations" - counting all 15 pushes UP (41.1), counting 14 pushes UP (40.5, not an option); "35 seconds" - as 0.35 minute pushes DOWN (36.9); the 4.8 km not subtracted from 23.6 pushes UP (46.2, not an option). One distractor per clause; none from ignoring a clause.

36.9.error_type: other: seconds read as decimal minutes

stops only at stations other than the two end stations
35-second stop at each of those stations

topic_tag: cost per bus trip for a month with a partly employer-paid pass, express surcharges and trips counted from a calendar
subskill: unit cost from a counted calendar
prompt: Leo rides the city bus with a monthly pass. This March has 31 days, and March 1 is a Sunday. On each weekday (Monday through Friday) Leo rides the bus to work and back home, except on Monday, March 16, a holiday, when he does not ride at all. On every Wednesday he also rides from home to the gym and back. On every Saturday he rides the bus to a class but gets a ride home, so he rides only one way. He takes no other bus rides. The March pass costs $96.50, and his employer pays $31.25 of that. On 3 of the days he works, Leo takes the express bus to work and back, and each express ride carries a $1.35 surcharge on top of the pass. Counting each one-way ride as one trip, what is Leo's cost per trip for March, to the nearest cent?
explanation: March 1 is a Sunday, so the weekdays are March 2-6, 9-13, 16-20, 23-27 and 30-31: 22 weekdays, of which 21 are workdays after the holiday, giving 42 work trips. subskill: rates from paces over repeating intervals
prompt: In a 10-kilometer race, Hana uses a run-walk plan: starting at the start line, she runs for 4 minutes, then walks for 1 minute, and repeats this pattern until she crosses the finish line. She runs at a steady pace of 5 minutes 48 seconds per kilometer and walks at a steady pace of 11 minutes 6 seconds per kilometer. To the nearest tenth of a minute, what is Hana's finishing time for the race?
explanation: Running pace 5 min 48 s = 5.8 min/km, so 4 minutes of running covers 4/5.8 = 0.68966 km; walking pace 11 min 6 s = 11.1 min/km, so 1 minute of walking covers 1/11.1 = 0.09009 km. One 5-minute cycle covers 0.77975 km, and 12 full cycles cover 9.35695 km in 60 minutes. The remaining 0.64305 km is less than one 4-minute run (0.68966 km), so she finishes while running: 0.64305(5.8) = 3.730 minutes. Finishing time 63.730, or 63.7, minutes. The option 64.1 scales the cycle time in proportion, 10/0.77975 cycles x 5 minutes, as if the last part were covered at the average pace. The option 68.6 averages the two paces over time, (4(5.8) + 11.1)/5 = 6.86 min/km, instead of over distance. The option 60.9 reads 5 min 48 s and 11 min 6 s as 5.48 and 11.06 minutes.

prompt: Two identical buoys float on the same series of waves. topic_tag: expected value
subskill: expected waiting time for an irregular schedule
prompt: On weekday mornings, a shuttle leaves a station at exactly 7:04, 7:15, 7:27, 7:33, 7:51, and 8:14 a.m., and at no other times between 7:00 and 8:14 a.m. Mia arrives at the station at a random time between 7:00 a.m. and 8:00 a.m., with every moment in that hour equally likely, and she waits for the next shuttle to leave. To the nearest hundredth of a minute, what is the expected number of minutes Mia waits?
explanation: Split the hour by departure times. If Mia arrives during an interval that ends at a departure, her wait runs evenly from the interval's length down to 0, so her average wait there is half the length: 7:00-7:04 (4 min, average 2), 7:04-7:15 (11, 5.5), 7:15-7:27 (12, 6), 7:27-7:33 (6, 3), 7:33-7:51 (18, 9). From 7:51 to 8:00 (9 min) the next shuttle is at 8:14, so her wait runs from 23 down to 14 minutes, average 18.5. Weighting each average by the interval's share of the 60 minutes: (4(2) + 11(5.5) + 12(6) + 6(3) + 18(9) + 9(18.5))/60 = 487/60 = 8.12. The option 7.33 averages the six interval averages without weighting by length. The option 6.02 treats 8:00 as if a shuttle left then, so the last interval averages 4.5. The option 9.75 uses the whole 23-minute gap from 7:51 to 8:14 (average 11.5) while still dividing by 60.

prompt: A shuttle company accepts 12 reservations for a van ride that has 10 passenger seats. Each person with a reservation shows up for the ride with probability 0.85, independently of the other people. Every person who shows up but cannot get a seat receives a $20 travel voucher. To the nearest cent, what is the expected total value, in dollars, of the vouchers given out for this ride?
explanation: Let K be the number of people who show up; K is binomial with n = 12 and p = 0.85. Vouchers are given only if K = 11 (1 voucher) or K = 12 (2 vouchers). P(K = 12) = 0.85^12 = 0.1422 and P(K = 11) = 12(0.85^11)(0.15) = 0.3012. The expected number of vouchers is 1(0.3012) + 2(0.1422) = 0.5856, so the expected value is 20(0.5856) = 11.71 dollars. The option 8.87 pays one $20 voucher whenever the van is overbooked, 20(0.3012 + 0.1422). The option 6.19 leaves out the factor 12 in P(K = 11) (counting only one order of who stays home). The option 26.43 is off by one seat: it counts a voucher when 10 people show up, 20(1 P(K = 10) + 2 P(K = 11) + 3 P(K = 12)).

topic_tag: iterating a complex quadratic map
subskill: recursive complex sequence

The option "3.16" forgets to add c in the last step, giving |z₂²| = |z₂|² ≈ 3.16. The option "1.78" stops one step early and gives |z₂|. The option "1.82" squares without doubling the cross term, (a + bi)² = a² − b² + abi, at both steps.

The option 698 halves the least outside diameter, 87.5/2 = 43.75, and then subtracts twice the wall thickness from that radius, giving 42.15 cm. The option 738 subtracts the wall thickness only once from the diameter, giving an inside diameter of 87.5 − 0.8 = 86.7 cm.

topic_tag: orbital speed with mixed length units and a minutes-seconds period
subskill: orbit radius from km radius plus mile altitude; speed in km/h
prompt: A satellite travels in a circular orbit 254 miles above Earth's surface. Earth is modeled as a sphere with a radius of 6,371 kilometers, and the satellite completes one orbit every 92 minutes 41 seconds. Using 1 mile = 1.609344 kilometers, what is the satellite's speed, to the nearest kilometer per hour?
explanation: The orbit's radius is Earth's radius plus the altitude: 6,371 + 254(1.609344) ≈ 6,371 + 408.77 = 6,779.77 kilometers, so one orbit is 2π(6,779.77) ≈ 42,598.4 kilometers. The period is 92 + 41/60 ≈ 92.683 minutes ≈ 1.54472 hours, so the speed is 42,598.4/1.54472 ≈ 27577 kilometers per hour. The option 26947 adds the 254 miles to the radius without converting it to kilometers. The option 26556 converts the altitude by dividing by 1.609344 instead of multiplying (157.83 kilometers). The option 27658 reads 92 minutes 41 seconds as 92.41 minutes.
